overview: This map record spans more than one formal British name. England and Scotland formed the Kingdom of Great Britain in 1707; union with Ireland made the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland in 1801. Mills, steam engines and an enormous empire created wealth and new travel, but relied on colonial extraction and enslaved labor. A Georgian child, a Manchester mill family and an Irish family during famine did not live the same story. The imported 1715 to 1878 map interval is a slice, not the whole country’s life.

periods.title: A contested union
periods.summary: England and Scotland formed Great Britain with one Parliament in 1707. Scottish opposition, new taxes and rival loyalties showed that a legal union did not produce instant agreement.

periods.title: Households, empire and experiments
periods.summary: Georgian households, schools and medical practice differed by wealth and place. British trade and collecting also drew on plantation slavery and colonial power.

periods.title: Machines and the Irish union
periods.summary: Steam-powered industry and Manchester cotton grew. The 1800 union laws brought Ireland into a new United Kingdom from 1801; the 1707 Great Britain title no longer described the whole state.

periods.title: Factories, railways and abolition
periods.summary: Factories and railways reshaped travel and work. Parliament banned the British slave trade in 1807 and abolished slavery in most colonies in the 1830s, with compensation paid to slaveholders.

periods.title: Famine and uneven reform
periods.summary: The Irish Great Famine brought hunger and migration. Some cities built public toilets and schools, but access was unequal. The map slice stops in 1878 without any national ending.

periods.title: Beyond this map slice
periods.summary: The British state continued beyond 1878. Another map record covers later British history; this endpoint records imported coverage, not a collapse.

items.text: The 1707 union joined England and Scotland as Great Britain, with one Westminster Parliament. Wales was already included with England; Ireland remained a separate kingdom, so calling the new 1707 state “the UK of Great Britain and Ireland” would jump nearly a century ahead.

Not everyone cheered. Scotland’s Parliament ratified the articles amid public protests; new taxes caused more anger. Families could share a king and Parliament yet disagree fiercely about what those institutions should do.

The 1800 Acts of Union took effect on 1 January 1801. Ireland lost its separate Parliament and entered a UK with Great Britain. Irish objections and later self-government campaigns make it important to say whose political voice the union strengthened or denied.

In a wealthy Georgian townhouse, a basement kitchen and service rooms could separate household labor from formal rooms upstairs. A servant’s daily route through the home was different from the family’s; many rural families lived and worked in quite different spaces.

Quakers took over the former Ackworth Foundling Hospital in 1778 for a boarding school. One teacher might use older or more advanced pupils as monitors for small groups. The example shows expanding education, not that every child attended school.

In eighteenth-century Bristol, Pero was brought from Nevis as an enslaved servant in a merchant’s household. His life is a reminder that “Georgian Britain” included Black people and that colonial slavery was connected to a British family’s front door.

Watt and Boulton improved steam engines for industrial power; they did not invent steam itself. In Manchester, machines spun cotton into cloth while much raw cotton was grown by enslaved people overseas. An invention can be ingenious and still sit inside an unjust supply chain.

In Manchester’s Ancoats, archaeologists found a wooden domino from workers’ housing: someone had time for a game amid crowded streets and mills. In 1831 cholera struck, and more than half its houses lacked plumbing. A game piece and a drain tell different parts of one neighborhood’s story.

Physician and collector Hans Sloane promoted inoculation against smallpox. His collections helped start the British Museum, while his wealth and collecting were tied to slavery in Jamaica. Scientific curiosity and imperial exploitation could occupy the same life.

Archaeologists found a decorated Georgian chamber pot at East Tilbury, dating roughly 1765 to 1795. Not everyone had a flushing toilet a few steps from bed: a pot was portable, but someone still had the unpleasant job of emptying it. This is one local find.

At the Great Exhibition of 1851, visitors could pay a penny to use installed toilets. London later opened municipal public toilets, but facilities for women remained far scarcer. A useful invention is less useful if you are not allowed through the door.

Potato blight devastated Irish crops from 1845, but starvation and mass emigration were also shaped by poverty and government choices. Ireland was part of this UK: its famine belongs in British state history, not in a footnote outside it.

sections.title: A line of writing and a map boundary

items.text: The 1707 Articles said Scotland and England would be “united into one kingdom by the name of Great Britain.” This is a short sample of written English from a state document, not a claim that everyone in Britain spoke or wrote only English.

The 1870 Education Act allowed school boards in England and Wales; Scotland received a related act in 1872. Attendance was not made compulsory for five-to-ten-year-olds until 1880, and poorer children often worked around school. The map ends at 1878 before that later milestone.

The imported map label “United Kingdom” covers both pre-1801 Great Britain and the early UK. The 1878 cutoff only changes which dataset record supplies a polygon. It does not mean the people, Parliament or state vanished that year.

ending.text: In 1801 the Kingdom of Great Britain was transformed by union with Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland. The political name changed; the people and institutions did not disappear. This imported map record continues to 1878 as a coarse coverage slice, and neither 1801 nor 1878 verifies its drawn borders.

sources.title: British Museum, Sir Hans Sloane
sources.note: Early eighteenth-century physician promoted smallpox inoculation; his collection helped found British Museum and was entangled with Jamaican plantation slavery.

sources.note: Ackworth Quaker boarding school 1778 and Georgian school arrangements, including monitors and small schoolrooms; examples not universal schooling.

sources.note: Georgian urban townhouses could separate basement kitchens and service spaces from reception rooms; class-specific built environment.

sources.note: Watt and Boulton steam engines used for industrial power in late eighteenth-century Birmingham; later factory growth; Watt improved engines, did not invent steam.

sources.title: Historic England, Black Lives in England: Servants

sources.note: British participation in slave trade; 1807 trading ban, 1833 abolition statute effective 1834; owners compensated, formerly enslaved people not.

sources.title: Science and Industry Museum, 1830: A rebellious year
sources.note: 1830 Liverpool and Manchester Railway alongside industrial cotton growth, mill hardship and demands for representation.

sources.note: Manchester Ancoats workers housing, archaeological domino, 1831 cholera and more than half of houses lacking plumbing; local case.

sources.title: UK Parliament, The Great Famine
sources.note: Irish Great Famine 1845-52, potato blight, starvation, illness, mass emigration and British government response; avoid reducing causes to crop disease alone.

sources.title: Historic England, Public Conveniences at Guilford Place
sources.note: 1851 Great Exhibition charged one penny to use toilets; 1855 London municipal facilities; Victorian women had much poorer public access.

sources.title: UK Parliament, The 1870 Education Act
sources.note: School boards in England and Wales 1870, similar Scottish law 1872, compulsory attendance five to ten in 1880, fees to 1891; poor children often worked.

sources.note: British empire and independence chronology, including Indian independence 1947 and multiple African and Caribbean states 1957-70; colonies had their own peoples and agency.
